newsitem.title: USA: 'Got-a-hunch, bet-a-bunch' traders having tough time.
newsitem.headline: 'Got-a-hunch, bet-a-bunch' traders having tough time.

text.p: Market timers -- those brave souls who are eternally trying to outguess the direction of stocks with their 'Got-a-hunch, bet-a-bunch-type' of investing -- are having a tough time in Wall Street's volatile trading environment.

Indeed, the traders who jump in and out of stocks, looking to sell ahead of a market correction and buy on the cheap, have been especially nervous this summmer as the Dow Jones industrial average has swung unpredictably.

"It's like trying to find a needle in not one hay stack but in an entire silo of hay," said James O'Shaughnessy, president of O'Shaughnessy Capital Management, and author of the book, 'What works on Wall Street' (McGraw-Hill).
Stocks have been on a fast-track since 1995 as Wall Street enjoyed the near perfect climate of lower interest rates, subdued inflation and strong corporate profits.
But as stocks soared to dizzying heights, market gurus, sensing that the market was over-pricing stocks, predicted the end was near for the Dow's spectacular rise.
The mighty Dow index proved the experts wrong as it finished 1995 with its biggest gain ever, jumping nearly 40 percent to 5,117.12.
This year from January through May, the index of 30-blue-chip companies set 21 record highs, striking a milestone of 5,778.00 on May 22, which was quickly followed by a slide to 5,182.32 by July 16.
Analysts said that the market's wild swings have been aggravated by market timers, whose trading strategy is viewed as the closest thing to a coin-toss.

In a rising market, the traders pick a top for stocks on the belief that people will not want to pay up for the shares. On the other hand, in a falling market, they pick a bottom and assume that no one will want to sell below certain levels.
At times, the traders are right when the risky trades go their way, but statistically, the market almost never gives them the "right stuff" over and over again.
O'Shaughnessy said that in the last 25 years of stock market shakeouts, the traders have been out of the money.
"In the crash between 1973 to 1974, people who were out of the market thought, 'I'm so brilliant being out of the market and I'm in cash,'" he said.

"The problem was when the market came roaring back in 1975, almost all of the gains happened for that year in a very compressed time period during a couple of months and it did not give the market timers enough time to get back in," O'Shaughnessy said.
He said that in the 1987 crash, the traders were selling stocks after the market broke down, when in fact, they should have been buying.

"The whole notion of market timers is that they are smarter than the other players, but few are going to be able to do it with any great success because what generally happens is that some extremely volatile event will occurr," he said.
O'Shaughnessy said long-term traders have always done better than the short-term speculators whose trading is largely based on emotions.
"Speculators make pennies, investors make dollars, he said.
In late trading Friday, the Dow was up 68.80 points at 5,675.76. For the week, it was up 59.55 points after losing 106.53 points in the prior week.
